question: Why does test_rewrite_ast employ pytest.register_assert_rewrite() in the package's __init__.py rather than relying solely on the automatic conftest-based rewriting mechanism, and what does this reveal about the design architecture?
answer:
Because pytest's automatic rewriting only covers `conftest.py` files, test modules matching the `python_files` patterns, and registered plugins — not arbitrary helper modules. Any module imported before pytest's `AssertionRewritingHook` (a `sys.meta_path` import hook) can rewrite it is already cached in `sys.modules` and can never be rewritten, triggering the "Module already imported so cannot be rewritten" warning. `pytest.register_assert_rewrite()` adds the module to the hook's mandatory-rewrite registry before its first import, and putting that call in the package's `__init__.py` is the only guaranteed ordering point, since Python always imports a package's `__init__.py` before any submodule; conftest.py loading happens later (during collection) and its "automatic rewriting" applies only to the conftest file itself, so it cannot reliably cover helpers imported at package-import time.

This reveals that pytest's assertion rewriting is deliberately an opt-in, import-time, name-registry mechanism layered on Python's import system — not a global static transform of all source files — keeping rewriting scope controlled for performance and to avoid touching third-party code. It also shows pytest dogfoods its own public extension API: its test suite exercises the same plugin-style mechanisms offered to users, validating the public contract from the outside.
